speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I wish to draw Members' attention to the Standing Orders before the Motion is proceeded with.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Members are hence reminded that they should confine their observations to the subject of the Motion to be discussed.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Any aspersions on the conduct of the former Speaker or allegations that he was thereby not independent and impartial will hence be out of order.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Members are to abide by these Standing Orders and I will disallow any remarks which infringe the rules.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We are sure that your years of experience as Deputy Speaker will put you in good stead for the role that has now been entrusted to you and we trust that you will do your best to restore public confidence in the office of the Speaker of Parliament.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The events that led us to debate this Motion today has been truly regrettable.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In carrying out these important duties, the Speaker must remain impartial to all Members of Parliament (MPs), regardless of their political affiliation.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: He must be seen as a fair referee, just like a Judge.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Mr EW Barker, the first Law Minister of Independent Singapore, pointed out the similarities between the Speaker of Parliament and a Judge during a speech in this House in January 1970.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Mr Barker said, and I quote, "There is a great deal of similarity between the Judge and the Speaker.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The impartiality both are expected to maintain between contending and contentious factions has to be, it is generally believed, judicial." Indeed, all Speakers of Parliament prior to 1970 had been members of the legal profession, a fact that was also pointed out by Mr Barker in his speech.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is paramount that a Speaker must be impartial and be seen by the public as impartial in discharging his duties in this House.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Speaker Tan's comment during the 17 April Sitting already damaged the public perception of its impartiality, even before the revelation of his inappropriate relation with a fellow PAP Member of Parliament (MP).

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Let us consider the context of Speaker Tan's comments.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Assoc Prof Jamus Lim had just concluded a speech on poverty, titled "Hard Living in Singapore".

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Among other things, he called for the implementation of a poverty line and to make the approval process for ComCare less onerous and intrusive.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: After Assoc Prof Jamus Lim had taken a seat, Speaker Tan muttered a comment under his breath which I will not repeat, out of respect for the Standing Orders.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Speaker Tan's comments were highly contentious for two reasons.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: First, unparliamentary profanities were used in the comment.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Speaker of Parliament is, of course, entitled to form his own private opinions on any Member of this House or any speeches made here.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, as an impartial referee that enforces Parliamentary rules and procedures, the Speaker must not publicly express those opinions.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is no different from judges and heads of states in the Westminster system.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We do not expect or, indeed, allow judges to express their opinions publicly or heads of states to express a different view from the government on public policy.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The issue here is that not being neutral and impartial leads to consequences of negative public perception that lower public trust in public institutions.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While Speaker Tan may not have expected that his comment will be picked up publicly, he was on duty and discharging his responsibilities as Speaker of the House.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It was, therefore, a serious error to have even made that comment.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Furthermore, the tone and content of the comment make it clear that Speaker Tan objected to the contents of Assoc Prof Jamus Lim's speech.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is especially problematic because the Speaker is expected to ensure that Parliament is a fair arena for all MPs, regardless of their political affiliation and he was objecting to the speech made by a Member of a different political party.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Leong, if I can just remind you what I mentioned at the start, before you spoke, that we should not be comment – this is not a debate on the conduct of former Speaker Tan Chuan-Jin.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But the recent event is, sort of, the ingredient for bringing out the principle, right?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, it is part and parcel of —

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: But not to comment on the conduct of former Speaker Tan Chuan-Jin.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Speaker Tan's comment thus did great damage to public perception of his impartiality as well as the impartiality of the office of the Speaker.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: He acknowledged this in his resignation letter to Prime Minister Lee when he said that his mistake raised "broader questions over my neutrality and impartiality as Speaker." Speaker Tan's inappropriate comments —

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I thought you understood what I said earlier?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Yes, but this is part and parcel of —

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: So, you can talk about your Motion, which is about the neutrality of the Speaker, but you do not need to make references to the conduct of former Speaker Tan Chuan-Jin.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Can I know under what Standing Order I am restricted from saying this?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Speaker Tan's comments are a direct strike at the values that underpin this Parliament, as a result we are —

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: So, these are the specific references that you asked for.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: We think the Speaker should be held to a higher standard than an MP.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: This is an issue that should be debated further in this House.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: For any democracy to function properly, it must function on the basis of a Parliament that it can trust.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: How can the public trust Parliament when its presiding officer had compromised his ability to be independent and impartial?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: As I mentioned earlier, prior to 1970, all the Speakers of Parliament had been members of the legal profession, either judges or lawyers.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Except for the brief period between 1963 and 1964, when Mr EW Barker was Speaker of Parliament, all the Speakers of Parliament were also non-partisan.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: When Mr Barker was elected as Speaker, Deputy Prime Minister Dr Toh Chin Chye explained that this was a temporary stop-gap measure until the consent of the Malaysian government, which was responsible for Singapore's judiciary at the time, when we were part of the Federation of Malaysia, could be solved, for a judge to be elected as Speaker.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: And indeed, this was followed through when AP Rajah was elected as Speaker in November 1964.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: However, this convention changed after 1970, following the election of PAP backbencher and non-lawyer, Dr Yeoh Ghim Seng, as Speaker.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Since 1970, the office of Speaker has been occupied by a PAP MP.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Furthermore, in recent years, Speaker Tan and his predecessors have also been members of the Central Executive Committee (CEC) of the PAP.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: In other words, at the power centre of the ruling party.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: This evolution from having a non-partisan Speaker, a backbencher Speaker, to Speakers who are ex-office holders or members of the PAP's CEC could be perceived as having eroded the independence and impartiality of the Speaker's office over the years.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: PSP believes that it is problematic for the Speaker to uphold his impartiality and independence while simultaneously being at the power centre of the ruling party and being privy to the ruling party's political strategy alongside members of the Government.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Hence, we supported the elevation of Mr Speaker from the backbenches to the Speaker's office this time round.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: We hope that the Speaker of Parliament, who is not closely linked to the core of the PAP, will be able to restore public confidence in the impartiality and independence of the office of the Speaker of Parliament.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The PSP trusts, that you, Mr Speaker, will make every effort to do this for the rest of this term of Parliament.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: In 1642, King Charles I of England entered the English House of Commons and attempted to arrest five MPs.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: He demanded that the Speaker of Commons, William Lenthall, identify these five Members for arrest.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Lenthall famously replied to the King, "May it please Your Majesty, I have neither eyes to see nor tongue to speak in this place, except as the House, whose servant I am, directs of me." This incident underlines the principle that the Speaker should not be subordinate to the Government but an independent servant of the House.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The Speaker has a duty to this House and this House alone.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: He is also not at liberty to express his opinions beyond defending the interests of this House.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The comments of a Speaker, therefore, must continue to build on the confidence that the public has in the office of the Speaker and he must always be independent and impartial.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The position of the Speaker of Parliament exists in almost all modern parliamentary systems.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The Speaker is a generally a Member of the House that is selected by fellow Members with a majority of the vote.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: While Singapore’s Constitution does not require the Speaker to be a Member of Parliament (MP), the general practice has been for the Speaker to be an elected Member.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In most countries, the result of these two practices, namely (a) the Speaker being an MP and (b) the Speaker being elected by the majority of the House is often that the Speaker is an MP from the ruling party.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: There are times when non-ruling party MPs get elected as Speaker, and in Singapore's case, when non-MPs also get elected as Speakers, but this is the exception rather than the rule.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: PSP's proposal does not seem to be suggesting we do away with this completely, but just seems to suggest within certain parameters around which the person should be selected, namely that the individual should not have been a part of the core leadership team of the ruling party.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I do not think there is the need for this additional limitation and I will explain this in my speech.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The Speaker has the duty to preside over the elected representatives in the Chamber and he must in turn have their mandate to do so.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Otherwise, you will have the anomalous situation of an unelected person potentially controlling the proceedings of the elected officials.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I think while my colleague Mr Leong highlighted some similarities between the role of a Judge and the role of a Speaker, there are also some important differences.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: One of the most important differences is that a Judge makes decisions on the facts before them and their decisions bind all parties on those facts.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The Speaker, on the other hand, presides over Parliamentary proceedings, and while the Speaker may make decisions on procedural issues, the substantive decisions are made by the legislative chamber itself.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Bills can only be passed by elected representatives.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The Speaker does not have the power to force a Bill through.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Since Independence though, Singapore, like the UK and all other Commonwealth countries, had its own Parliament and the Speaker was one who was voted in by the majority of legislators in Parliament.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: As a matter of practice, the Speaker was nominated by the Prime Minister since the Prime Minister is the individual who commands the support of the majority in the House.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The Speaker in Singapore does not have to be from the ruling party, but usually is.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: After Sir George Oehlers, our next Speaker was Mr EW Barker in 1963 and he was also a very successful lawyer.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But he was a member of the ruling party.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Following that, from 1970, we had three of our longest serving Speakers: Dr Yeoh Ghim Seng, Mr Tan Soo Khoon and Mr Abdullah Tarmugi.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The three of them took us all the way from 1970 to 2011.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In Mr Abdullah Tarmugi's case, he was a member of the Cabinet, so, he was a part of the core leadership team before becoming a Speaker.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: They were appointed the same way as their predecessors, namely, nominated by the Prime Minister and elected by the House.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The fact that the Speaker is from the ruling party is not something that should take away from the discharge of their duties.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The Speaker is still required to discharge their duties independently and impartially.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The Motion talks about Parliament being a fair arena.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: However, the fairness of Parliament is not just dependent on the individual who is the Speaker.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The Speaker himself, like all Members, is bound by Parliament's Standing Orders as well as the Parliament (Privileges, Immunities and Powers) Act.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Parliament's Standing Orders give Members who wish to speak a wide range of opportunities to do so.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: They may file Parliamentary Questions for written or oral answer, which Ministers will have to address publicly.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: They may speak on any Bills put forward by the Government, meaning, they have a say on any and every piece of legislation that passes this House.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: They may file Adjournment Motions if they need more time to speak on a specific issue and, again, the relevant Ministry will be required to address the issues raised.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The Parliament (Privileges, Immunities and Powers) Act sets out additional protections for MPs, including freedom of speech such that anything that is said in Parliament is generally protected from proceedings in Court or any other forum, other than Parliament itself, which is why the Parliament is the first port of call if Members were to breach the Standing Orders.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: All these matters provided for in Parliament's Standing Orders give every Member, whether from the ruling party or the opposition, the opportunity to raise and discuss matters they feel are important.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In keeping Parliament a fair arena, it is therefore also important for all Members to respect and comply with these rules.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The substance of keeping Parliament a fair arena is, I would respectfully say, largely captured in these rules and the law.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: If, indeed, there is any allegation that the Speaker has not acted independently and impartially in his decisions, this should be the subject of a specific Motion.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The first is the Speaker's own party, if it feels the Speaker has not acted properly in any way.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The second is Parliament itself, where Members are free to raise any objections they may wish to or even file the necessary Motion.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Third, the ultimate check on a Member of the legislature is the ballot box.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: As Parliamentary debates are public, every action that the Speaker may take is up for public scrutiny.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: If there is any allegation that he has been unfair or impartial in the discharge of his duties, that is something the voters may take into account, both against him and even the party he is from, if the party endorses that conduct.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I think Mr Leong has made some references to the UK and the Speaker there.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I would say different countries may have different practices in selecting the Speaker.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The UK has a practice of the Speaker resigning from his political party upon nomination and actually being "dragged", supposedly unwillingly, from this chair to take the seat of the Speaker.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This is because of the history of the Speaker sometimes having to deliver uncomfortable news to the Crown and for which he may face the consequences.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: However, even though the Speaker may resign from his party upon nomination, it is clear that he still has the support of the party that commands the majority in Parliament and, in most cases, was a former member of that party.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: That would suggest his personal beliefs are likely to be aligned with the party he was a member of.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Notwithstanding that, in the discharge of his duties, he is expected to be independent and impartial.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: There are other peculiarities in the UK's approach, including that the Speaker's seat is generally uncontested by other parties and he campaigns as Speaker.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: He is thus likely to get re-elected unchallenged if campaigning as a Speaker.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This means that, unlike the Singapore system, where people vote for all legislators, including the Speaker, in the UK, the Speaker would not be subject to a challenge at the ballot box.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, his accountability in that sense is only to the Parliament itself, should the majority nominate him again.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This is a different approach, but I do not think it is necessarily superior to the one we have.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: There are other Commonwealth Countries, such as Australia, which have a system very similar to ours.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: There, the Speaker remains a member of a political party and will have to campaign for re-election like any other Member.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The Speaker needs to get the support from the majority in Parliament.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In practice, most of the Speakers have been from the ruling party, although there, too, were a few notable exceptions – just like in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The Speaker in the Australian Parliament has often had to exercise a much firmer hand than the Speaker in Singapore on Points of Order and breaches of the Standing Orders of Parliament.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It is important for Members to respect the Standing Orders so that other Members would also have opportunities to speak and raise the points they need to speak.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It is thus important for all Members to honour and comply with their obligations as set out in the Standing Orders as well as the Parliament (Privileges, Immunities and Powers) Act.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Can I have a copy of your amendment?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: I will just wait for Members to get the copies.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Vikram Nair, you can move your amendment.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: This is being suggested so that the Motion is not misinterpreted to mean that the Speaker cannot be from a political party in order to be independent.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: The amendment therefore focuses on the independence in the discharge of his duties, which is the standard Speakers in all Parliamentary systems are held to.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: The Speakers in many Commonwealth Parliamentary systems come from the ruling party and this has never been a basis to say Parliament is not a fair arena for debate.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: The second part of the amendment is, I think, equally important.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: These are rules that every Member should be committed to in our shared obligation to ensure Parliament is a fair arena.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: I therefore beg to move the Motion as amended, Mr Speaker.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: There are three amendments proposed by Mr Vikram Nair to the Motion.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: It may be convenient that the debate on the original Motion and on any other amendments moved by Members be proceeded with simultaneously as a debate on a single question.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While any call for censure of the former Speaker would appear to have been overtaken by events, I would like to offer some thoughts on two matters: first, on the reaction to the speech, and second, on the role of debate in policymaking in a modern democracy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The former Speaker had characterised the proposals I offered on policies targeted at alleviating the plight of the poor as populist.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Everyone is entitled to their opinion, of course, and I do not fault him for having his own views on the matter.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: That said, I will only add that populist policies are those designed to appeal to the broad populace – hence, the name – who feel aggrieved by the establishment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Populism is about arousing the raw sentiment, with a perception of an uncaring elite.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To be clear, my intention was anything but.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Rather, I was speaking up for a group that, by definition, is a minority.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I would have hoped that it should not be seen as an effort to rally mass outrage, but an effort to flag concerns for a group that is often voiceless.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: When we were a developing nation, the sorts of optimal policies we should pursue – the pursuit of an economy open to international trade and investment flows, coupled with an orientation toward export promotion, for instance, or a keen respect for the rule of law and property rights, along with the importance of governance, more generally, and socio-political stability, undergirded by meritocratic principles and respect for the equality of different races and religions – were well understood, even if non-trivial to accomplish.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Thanks to the pioneering generation of Singapore's leaders, however, we were able to build a foundation of economic openness, institutional quality and social capital, which we as subsequent generations have been able to draw on and enjoy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: These were the ingredients for Singapore's economic success, and it has made us into one of the richest economies in the world.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While we should never allow the legacy of these hard-won policies and institutions to erode, the reality of a modern economy and society is that the way forward is no longer as certain.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While many of the challenges of development were about getting these fundamentals right, the issues faced by a developed nation do not present as clear-cut a solution.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Think about matters that now occupy much of our political and Parliamentary time.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Issues like the need for greater social protection through the institution of a minimum wage, official poverty line or unemployment insurance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Or a more vibrant intellectual environment that will allow our highly trained workforce the room to be creative and innovative.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Or greater equality in sharing the fruits of our economic success via more progressive income and wealth taxation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is because I sincerely believe that we will only arrive at a balance that society as a whole can accept when there is some degree of agitation toward a solution, and even if some may do so somewhat more grudgingly.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This brings me back to our former Speaker's original remark.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This can only happen in a Parliamentary setting where such differences of opinion are not only acquiesced to, but actually welcomed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Do we deride what we disagree with and dismiss it with a convenient label or seek to score political points with ad hominem rebuttals or do we at least seek to understand the premise of the other's argument, giving them the benefit of the doubt even if we may ultimately disagree with them?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Can this occur anywhere, but in a Chamber where Members feel that the freedom to air these alternative views, with an adjudicator that they feel is independent and impartial?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This comes down to a competition in ideas and I do not believe any single person in this House will always have the best ones.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Academics, of which I am, are taught early on in their training to respect ideas, regardless of their origin.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: That is why we subject our work to seminars and conferences, to peer-reviewed journals and to public scrutiny, where they are challenged and, more frequently than we like, rejected.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As much as nobody enjoys having their ideas shot down, the process of defending, refining and revising our ideas is what makes them more robust and ultimately, far more valuable.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In the end, only the best ideas survive, and these are the ones that have the potential to go on and make a difference for both society and for the world at large.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: For the same reason, I believe we need greater competition in the politics, policies and ideas that will bring Singapore forward into the next century.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I will not be able to support the Motion as introduced by the NCMPs.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: While I agree that the Speaker of Parliament should be impartial and that Parliament should be a fair arena for debate, I cannot agree with the original Motion's call for the Speaker to be independent.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The term "independent" in the context of Parliament or in politics has a particular definition.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In his speech, Mr Leong appears to conflated the words "independent" and "impartial", but the fact that they both appear in the Motion suggests that they are intended to mean different things.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: When applied to a Member of Parliament (MP), the term "independent" would generally mean that that MP is not affiliated with a political party.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This definition is used not only in Singapore, but in most, if not all, Parliamentary democracies.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The Constitution does not require that a Speaker, whether drawn from MPs or non-MPs, to be independent.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Therefore, it is a non sequitur argument to expect that an MP elected as Speaker should resign from the party, he had been elected to Parliament with, as he would lose that seat.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: As such, this Motion, as it was originally crafted, would be envisioning a situation where only non-MP MPs who stood in the elections as independents and won, or Nominated Members of Parliament (NMPs) could be considered for the position of Speaker.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: First, there have never been independent MPs elected to the Singapore Parliament since Independence.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: So, this option can be dispensed with immediately.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Second, I have read media reports suggesting that NMPs be considered.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: But, Sir, we are, quite honestly, hardly a proper source, given that our term is only half of a Parliament's full term – although some of us may serve two terms, which is not usual – but we are not senior, nonetheless, to backbenchers with sufficient experience to chair the House and to carry out all the other roles of the Speaker.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: We would not want a revolving door of inexperienced Speakers.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In any event, given that Speakers do not take part in debates, it would be contrary to the objectives of having NMPs, which is to provide for alternative voices in Parliament.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: As regard to a non-MP serving as Speaker, there have been two such Speakers, as mentioned by hon Member Vikram Nair.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The first was Mr AP Rajah, who was the first Speaker of the Parliament of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: He was the holdover Speaker from the previous Legislative Assembly of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Rajah had at one time been a member of the Legislative Assembly and was an eminent lawyer.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: He later became an ambassador and a High Court Judge.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The second Speaker of Parliament, Mr Punch Coomaraswamy was also a non-MP.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Coomaraswamy was also an eminent lawyer and later also served as an ambassador and a High Court Judge.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I do not know the exact reason why the first two Speakers were non-MPs, but I can fathom that it may well be because Parliament was young at that time and wanted to have eminent local lawyers who would be familiar with formal procedure to chair the House in its early years.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Once MPs had sufficient experience, they were called upon to serve as Speakers and have done so until today.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: They have done a good job and their fairness has largely not been questioned by Members on both sides of the House.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Furthermore, even a cursory survey of current elected MPs would throw up many names who have the knowledge, experience, temperament and wisdom to serve as Speaker.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: It is only if we cannot find one within that we should look without.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: And we can find many elected MPs to take up the role.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This independent character of the Speaker was attained over a long, gradual and uneven process over 300 years, and it evolved in response to the particular political situation in the UK.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Members may know the origins of the position of the Speaker in the UK.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The Speaker is called the Speaker because he was the person appointed to speak to the King on behalf of the House of Commons.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The Speaker was expected to provide the King with the politically unvarnished views of the House.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: It was considered a dangerous position as Speakers were from time to time subject to the guillotine if the King was not happy with what the Speaker spoke.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Thankfully, Mr Speaker, Sir, this is no longer a hazard of that office or of your office.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: And it is in this regard that I will also take this opportunity to congratulate you in your elevation to the Chair.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The role of the Speaker in the UK has evolved with its independent nature solidified in both procedure and custom in the 19th century.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Such custom includes, for example, that an incumbent Speaker runs in the general elections not under a political party ticket but as Mdm or Mr Speaker in elections, and it is generally unopposed.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This custom is not something that is present in our system.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Most other jurisdictions that have a Westminster-type parliament also do not have an independent Speaker.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: India and Canada flirted with the idea, but both came to the conclusion that an MP who was elected as Speaker could be impartial without having to be independent.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The Canadian parliament rejected the notion that impartiality required independence and considered it a non sequitur argument – it was not considered an unreasonable expectation of the Speaker to separate his party allegiances with his duty to parliament.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: It also determined that it did not possess the customary nor procedural history that the UK had to support an independent Speaker – an argument I similarly make in relation to our House.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In India, the committee considering this question came to similar conclusions as the Canadian parliament.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In addition, the Indian Supreme Court had also opined on this matter and its pronouncement is worth mentioning because it sets out the underlying rational as to why a party-affiliated Speaker could still be impartial.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The court said: "The speaker, being a neutral person, is expected to act independently while conducting the proceedings of the house or adjudication of any petitions.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The constitutional responsibility endowed upon him has to be scrupulously followed, the court made it clear that his political affiliations cannot come in the way of adjudication." The court continued that if the Speaker is not able to disassociate from his political party and behaves contrary to the spirit of neutrality and independence, such person does not deserve to be reposed with public trust and confidence.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In other words, the court was saying that it is incumbent then on that house to invoke the relevant procedures to correct or, if necessary, to remove the Speaker.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: All this having been said, I come back to first principles – that is, that our Constitution does not require that our Speaker be independent.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: This is to ensure the orderly conduct of Parliamentary business.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Members of Parliament (MPs) can be arguing, quarrelling with one another.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: We note that in some countries, members of parliament fight in parliament.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: MPs can be criticising another person in public or in parliament, without giving them a fair chance of reply.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: This will be in breach of natural justice.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Time limits are set in Standing Orders because MPs can drag their speeches and, in the US, this is called filibuster.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Some of the older Members may remember Mr Lee Siew Choh who spoke seven hours in 1961 in the Singapore Legislative Assembly, and you then keep everyone occupied because you just want to extend the length of your speech and extend the time.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: So, many Parliaments, not just Singapore, set time limits on the length of speeches.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: So, I stress again, Mr Speaker, Standing Orders are important for the conduct of Parliamentary business.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: This part, I agree with that part of the Motion of Mr Leong Mun Wai.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: This is also clearly stated in the website of the Singapore Parliament.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The Speaker regulates and enforces the rule of debate.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: He decides who has the right to speak and puts the question for the House to debate on and to vote on.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The Speaker does not take part in the debates of the House but can abstain, vote for or against the Motion as if he has the original vote as an elected Member.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: During my five-year term, I was the Deputy Speaker to Speaker Mdm Halimah, now the President, and subsequently, I was Deputy Speaker to former Speaker, Mr Tan Chuan-Jin.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: As a Deputy Speaker, whenever I am required to preside over Parliament or to chair a Committee, I am always mindful of this need to ensure that I remain fair and impartial to all the Members in the House.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: So, I make sure that Members, whether they are from the ruling PAP party, the Opposition party or the NMPs, they are all given the chance to raise clarifications and to hold the Government to account.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: So, I am mindful that Parliament is a place for debate on policies and a good debate will allow better ideas to prevail and this would benefit all of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: As a Deputy Speaker, whenever I hear speeches made by	MPs from the PAP,	MPs from the Workers' Party, I, too, form my opinion on the contents of the speech, but I keep my views to myself.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: And as a Deputy Speaker, I know that I should not express my own view or even mutter my view under my breath.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: So, Sir, I want to add that the former Speaker, Mr Tan Chuan-Jin, has made known his stand to me and the other Deputy Speaker Mr Charles Chong that we have to be fair to all MPs, including members of the Workers' Party (WP), the NCMPs and the NMPs.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Over the past many years that I have been an MP, I have not heard of any MP within the House suggest that our Speaker has not been impartial.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: So, Sir, this is evidence that our Speaker is impartial in his conduct.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: He could have taken action against Mr Leong Mun Wai for behaving in a manner that was disrespectful and had disregarded authority.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: But he treated everyone fairly and he accepted the apology of Mr Leong and said that he concurred with the Leader's recommendation not to take further action on the matter.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: So, Mr Leong apologised, Speaker accepted it, and the matter was closed.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I would want to submit, Mr Speaker, that suggests very strongly that our Speaker has always been impartial.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Next, going to the point of Mr Leong's Motion that the Speaker must be independent, I am not sure how Mr Leong measures the term "independent".

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: If he suggests that "independent" means not being a member of a political party, then perhaps I can remind him of the former Speaker of the House of Commons, Mr John Bercow.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Mr John Bercow was a member of the UK Conservative Party before he resigned when he assumed the role of Speaker.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: However, even though he was not a member of the political party at the time, he was accused of not being impartial when he was Speaker.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: In fact, it was said he was refused a place in the House of Lords because he was not seen to be politically neutral.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: He was alleged to be biased against Brexit.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Thus, Mr Speaker, impartiality really depends on the person who is the Speaker and not his political affiliation.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: In many other Commonwealth countries, many Speakers are active members of their political parties.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Australian Speaker Mr Milton Dick is a member of the Labour Party, the Canadian Speaker is a member of the Liberal Party and the Speaker of the Lok Sabha India is a member of the Bharatiya Janata Party.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: So, even if we appoint a person who is without any political affiliation, whether the person is a judge or otherwise, I am quite certain that the person would have his or her own views of the speeches made by Members in the House.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Insofar as what he means by "independent" though, it was clear from his speech that, by "independent", he meant either non-partisan or not a member of a political party.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: So, to that extent, I cannot agree with this Motion.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The second part of Mr Leong's Motion seeks the House's affirmation that Parliament should be a fair arena for all.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: That, too, I agree, except that when it comes to being a fair arena for all, it means that all Members must participate in this and act and conduct themselves appropriately.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, let me move on to the first point about the need for the Speaker to be fair and impartial.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Speakers must behave in an impartial manner in the discharge of their duties and successive Speakers of our Parliament have acknowledged this.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The question is – how is this to be achieved?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The underlying assumption or presupposition put forward by PSP is that you can only achieve this if the Speaker is independent of any political party.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The premise is that the Speaker should not have any political association, so he or she can be perceived to be completely neutral.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Constitution sets out the eligibility requirements for the Speaker.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: MPs, except those who are Ministers or Parliamentary Secretaries, are eligible.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And non-MPs are also eligible, but the Constitution requires that such persons must be persons who are qualified for election as an MP, such as being a Singapore Citizen above the age of 21 and a resident in Singapore for at least 10 years in aggregate.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, our Constitution also recognises that MPs can be the Speaker, that is, members of a political party.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The second point is: what is the practice and the reality around the world?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And this is true of the current Speakers of the Australian House of Representatives, the Canadian House of Commons and the New Zealand House of Representatives, all of whom are from the majority party in those Parliaments.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In the US, the Speaker of the House of Representatives is also usually from the majority party in that House.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The identity of the Speaker is typically determined by the party members at the organising caucuses held soon after the new Congress is elected.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, in short, the Speaker is somebody who can receive the support from the majority of the House and that will very often be somebody from the majority party.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And this arrangement reflects the reality that the person has to receive a majority of the votes in Parliament to be appointed Speaker.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And it is quite natural for a candidate from the majority party to be in a position to receive the majority of votes.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It is also important to bear in mind that the majority party would have derived its majority from the voters.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: You do not get to be a majority party without the majority of votes.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It is the electorate; it is the voters who put the PAP in Parliament as a majority.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, you have to bear in mind that the mandate of the majority party is drawn directly from the people.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And the person put up for election as the Speaker, if he or she has the confidence of the majority, then he or she gets appointed as the Speaker.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And it is not always a given that a nominee from the majority party will always be able to command the support of the majority of the MPs or that the nominee may necessarily be from the majority party.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For example, the current Speaker of the US House of Representatives was appointed as Speaker only after 15 ballots were taken, despite receiving his party's nomination for Speaker earlier.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, for the first 14 ballots, he did not manage to obtain a majority of the votes.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This is not the only system in practice.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: There are different ways of doing it and our practice is in sync with other major democracies.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Each country has to decide what works best for them.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: More importantly, the Parliaments have to choose the right individuals.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, just having someone who is non-partisan or not a member of any political party does not guarantee you the outcome that you would like.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The convention also extends to the Speaker's seat not being contested by the major political parties and the Speaker not campaigning on political issues.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But even though the UK has taken these steps, that does not guarantee the desired outcomes.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As Mr Lim Biow Chuan highlighted earlier, the UK system did not prevent one of their former Speakers from being put in a position where he was accused of bias.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The former Speaker was mired in controversy by accepting certain procedural amendments and rulings.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I do not need to go into details, but in short, he was alleged of bias on issues, that is, of not supporting Brexit as opposed to remaining.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, you can have bias on issues or alleged bias on issues.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And also, he had separately had complaints levelled against him for bullying.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This does not have to do with his rulings in the Chamber, but he was the subject matter of an Independent Expert Panel.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And they found that his behaviour "fell very far below that which the public had a right to expect from any Member of Parliament", and it was so serious that, "had he still been a Member of Parliament" – because the Committee's rulings came out after he stepped down – the Committee said, "we would have determined that he should be expelled by resolution of the House.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As it is, we recommend that he should never be permitted a pass to the Parliamentary estate." So, having somebody who is non-partisan, not a member of a political party, does not guarantee you the results that you want.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But equally, it is important for the MPs to be mindful of the duties and obligations that come with their office – whether they be Ministers or backbenchers – and to not make it difficult for the Speaker, because in making it difficult for the Speaker, you also force the Speaker to have to make rulings.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It is incumbent upon MPs to not disregard the authority of the Chair, to be familiar with the Standing Orders, to know what the Standing Orders mean and, if referring to articles or principles or sections, to actually know which articles and sections they are referring to, and to not misrepresent proceedings in Parliament and essentially, comply with the Standing Orders.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, it works both ways for Parliament of function effectively, properly and importantly, to gain the respect of people.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Speaker has to do his job, but equally, all MPs and Ministers have to do their jobs.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It is about how the individual in the Speaker's Chair conducts himself or herself.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, for example, in 1995, Mr JB Jeyaretnam said when he spoke on the reappointment of Dr Yeoh Ghim Seng as Speaker, and Dr Yeoh, as Members know, was a PAP MP.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr JB Jeyaretnam said this, “Mr Speaker, Sir, may I, as it were from the other side of the House, give you my very sincere and hearty congratulations on your election.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We have heard from the Leader about your long reign in this House, but I, Mr Speaker, Sir, have only been under your rule for three years after I entered this House in December 1981.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But may I say, Mr Speaker, Sir, that during that short time of three years, you have gained greatly my respect and admiration for the charm and tact with which you brought to bear to this high office that you have hold with such esteem and honour.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It has not always been easy for you and sometimes it has been made trying, and my only hope is that I did not contribute in any way to your trials.” That was Mr JB Jeyaretnam.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Then, in 1989, Mr Chiam See Tong had this to say of Mr Tan Soo Khoon, who was Speaker and also a PAP MP – and not a lawyer.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Chiam said, "Mr Speaker, Sir, if you will just allow me a moment also to convey my congratulations on your elevation to the Speakership.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: It has allowed us to cover a little bit more ground than in the clarifications after a Ministerial Statement.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I will not rebut individually the points raised by some of the Members, but I would like to condense the thing in two points.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: One, we are here today – just now with the Ministerial Statement and now with this Motion – because something has happened.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: And that something is a very well-meaning speech and policy proposal put up by the Assoc Prof Jamus Lim that was just written-off in this House, in a very dismissive manner – although it is just a quiet comment.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But nevertheless, it is an indication that we need to remind ourselves on what is the impartiality of the Speaker.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Without that, we would not be debating today.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The second point I would like to make is, some of the Members who have spoken have talked about our Parliament, that we have an untainted record, track record of the Speaker being impartial, but here is an example that we have to remind ourselves that we need to reaffirm the impartiality of the Speaker.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: As a result of that, PSP had decided to put forward this Motion to suggest a gradual process whereby we can enhance the independence and impartiality of the Speaker, that this House would remember that in May this year, I actually have spoken about the rules and procedures of this House already, in my Adjournment Motion to make Parliament a fairer arena for all.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: At that time, I did not take up the issue of the independence and impartiality of the Speaker.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, the Motion is meant to propose a gradual process.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Of course, as our democracy develops and more and more members from different parties come into Parliament, then we can think of reverting to a situation whereby we have a totally independent Speaker.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: That is an ideal idea that PSP is trying to put forward with this Motion.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Parliament sits at the apex of our system of democracy.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: For it to function properly, the Members, processes and proceedings must all work towards promoting an environment where open, substantive and thorough debates can take place.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Well, I do not wish to go too much into Speaker Tan's case, actually, but just now I think what we have seen is that there are certain rules that this House has that has just prevented this Motion to be debated in a more open, substantive and thorough debate because of a technical point – that the Motion statement was not done in the way that allows me to have a more thorough debate.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: That is the current Standing Orders of the Singapore Parliament.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: These are all just incremental changes, and the Government can actually consider this and allow our Parliament to move closer to a fairer arena for all.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Hence, my Motion is meant to be a first step towards an independent and impartial Speaker and for Parliament to be a fairer arena for all.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The amended Motion on the other hand is re-affirming the status quo and just sticking to what is more of the same.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: And I have been debating in this House for the last three years that we cannot be just having the status quo.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Times have changed; the environment in the world has changed.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, why are we just sticking to the old rules, in many aspects of our Government?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, I view the two Motions as one.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: My Motion as a Motion with a dream, an objective that in the future, we can have a have a better Parliament.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, I hope this House will support my Motion.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The PAP Government does not need a super majority of about 90% to govern effectively, but such a super majority prevents the views and opinions of tens of thousands of loyal Singaporeans from being adequately represented in this House.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: (In Mandarin):   Dear fellow Singaporeans, today, we concluded the debate on the need for the Speaker of Parliament to be independent and impartial.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: This is a very important Motion, because Parliament sits at the apex of our democratic system, and the Speaker should be independent when presiding over Parliament proceedings and enforcing the Standing Orders to ensure that debates are carried out orderly.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: In carrying out his duties, he must be impartial and treat Members of Parliament (MPs) from different parties equally.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: He must be like a judge and be fair in executing Parliamentary procedures.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: We should learn from the recent incidents and find ways to plug the gaps, perfect the system and grow in the future.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: When we review the role of the Speaker over the years, we noticed that, compared to pre-Independence days, the impartiality and independence of the Speaker had changed quietly.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Since the People's Action Party (PAP) dominated Parliament, the office of Speaker has evolved from being occupied by a non-partisan person to a senior PAP member.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Before 1970, all Speakers of Parliament had been members of the legal profession.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: However, in 1970, when Dr Yeoh Ghim Seng, a PAP member and non-lawyer, became the Speaker, this convention changed.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I want to point out that this happened incidentally after the PAP captured 100% of the Parliamentary seats in the 1968 election.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Since 1970, the office of Speaker has been occupied by a PAP MP.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Furthermore, in recent years, Speaker Tan and his predecessor had also been members of the Central Executive Committee (CEC) of the PAP.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: In other words, although they held a politically neutral position, they were also at the power centre of the ruling party.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: We are glad to see that the new Speaker is not a PAP CEC member.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: As Singapore's democracy matures and the number of opposition MPs increases, we hope the Speaker will be a non-partisan person again like before.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: This will reflect progress in our democratic system and reverse the retrogressive practice of the PAP when appointing the Speaker over the past 50 plus years.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, Sir, under your leadership, we look forward to this House being a fairer arena for all.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: We have spent much Parliamentary time debating the issues and concerns of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: They have arisen from the recent spate of unfortunate events.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: It is my hope that in the coming months, there will be no more such events and this House can refocus our attention to the more important issues faced by Singaporeans, such as the rising cost of living, price and availability of public housing, economic uncertainty and job insecurity.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The first amendment is: "In line 1, after the word 'commitment', to insert '(a)'."

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The second amendment is: "In line 2, to delete 'be independent and impartial' and to insert the words 'discharge his duties independently and impartially'."

speaker: Mr Speaker
